items.title: Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here's why
items.description: Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act 's institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels. According to the National Apartment Association ’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse , released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction , the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out. The industry's legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects. Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry. “I would say it hasn't normalized. In other words, it wasn't where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences , said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD . “I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.” Uncertainty is still taking a toll Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position. “Capital's coming in, but it's not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it's really hard for them to write checks. According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group , a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets. Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere. “When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn't have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview. Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29. "Capital's just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market's still trying to find itself,” Tanner said. In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern. “Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned. The uncertainty surrounding Treasury’s proposed rulemaking The U.S. Department of the Treasury , which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations. “If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, 'all right, built-to-rent is carved out.' But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said. Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy. Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued. The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects. Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban. Supply Raleigh-Durham’s life sciences overall vacancy rate increased a modest 10 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 26.4% in Q3, despite quarterly occupancy gains. The increase reflected the removal of the RTP/I-40 Corridor’s 201,056-square-foot (sf) Charles Sanders Center, previously subleased to the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services, from the life sciences inventory following its lease to BASIS Independent Schools, removing it from the life sciences inventory. Vacancy remained 160 bps below its Q3 2025 peak of 28.0%, supported by occupancy gains in recently delivered buildings and declining sublease vacancy. Notably, sublease vacancy also improved by 70 bps year-over-year, falling from its record high of 3.6% in Q3 2025. Overall net absorption remained positive for the fourth consecutive quarter, bringing year-to-date (YTD) occupancy gains to more than 233,000 sf as tenant move-outs remained limited. Prior quarter leasing translated into Q3 move-ins, including Google Fiber occupying nearly 25,000 sf at Eastridge – Building 300 and Jazz Pharmaceuticals occupying more than 18,800 sf at TBC – Building 4020. Strong new leasing will continue to support occupancy gains, especially as large manufacturing users complete build outs of their spaces. Demand Nearly 130,000 sf of new leases were signed during Q3, bringing YTD activity to just under 397,000 sf. DG Matrix signed the quarter’s largest lease, taking nearly 55,000 sf at Southport 3 while diagnostics company Labcorp renewed for 33,500 sf at Eastridge – Building 100, contributing to nearly 64,000 sf of quarterly renewal activity. The RTP/I-40 Corridor submarket remained the primary driver of demand, representing 84.7% of new leasing YTD. Pricing Overall asking rates rose minimally QOQ, increasing by 0.3% to $38.63 per square foot (psf). Overall rates peaked at $40.31 psf in Q3 2023 when a wave of new, higher-priced space was introduced to the market. As premium space has leased, the market average has declined 4.2% from the peak. With construction paused and vacancy remaining elevated, asking rents are expected to remain relatively stable in the near term. items.description: Hottest outdoor storage property markets The numbers help explain the appetite. Rents for industrial outdoor storage roughly doubled across eight major markets between 2020 and the third quarter of this year, according to data from Newmark Research and Alterra IOS, an owner of such properties. Average rent per usable acre rose 103.5%, to nearly $11,000 a month, compared with a 66% increase for traditional industrial space, such as indoor warehouses. Rent growth, according to Alterra, is most closely tied to infrastructure and energy activity in the area, even more so than data center development specifically. The value of these properties can also increase if located near a seaport, rail line, or highway. But the gains weren't uniform. Baltimore (204%), Houston (159%) and Norfolk (148%) led, while South Florida and Savannah IOS actually trailed traditional industrial. Lisa DeNight, managing director, head of North American industrial research at Newmark, said that Savannah's IOS vacancy remains quite tight despite the rent figures. Recent port activity is a potential factor, according to Alterra. Savannah's container volumes more than doubled between 2010 and 2022 but have since declined, while Houston saw roughly 15% growth from 2022 to 2025. Sam Cheema co-founder of CanTex Capital, a Dallas-based firm that acquires overlooked industrial real estate in Texas, is seeing increased demand for these lots. "It comes down to supply and demand," he said. "If you need a warehouse you can usually find one. Properly zoned infill IOS sites are much harder to find and every year more of them are converted to warehouses and other uses," he said, referencing multifamily housing units. The scarcity makes tenants sticky. "So a limited supply keeps shrinking. And because so much of the value is in the land itself, owners keep the option to redevelop the site as the area grows," Cheema added. Because of the imbalance of supply and demand, rents and prices are rising across the board, according to Cheema, but no two IOS properties look alike, which has kept the door open for smaller investors. "Big institutions want exposure to IOS, but ownership is fragmented across mom-and-pop owners and small businesses, so it's hard to deploy large amounts of capital without first aggregating these assets into portfolios," Cheema said. Unlike traditional warehouses, there's no standard spec like square footage or clear height to compare them. "That lack of standardization along with the ongoing growth of the asset class, means there's still runway for small investors to find opportunities," Cheema said. "Financing has improved as more lenders have a better understanding of IOS, but it's still largely local and regional banks," Cheema added. Zoning is the biggest challenge. "If you don't understand the city's plans for the area, you may end up owning a use they're trying to phase out," Cheema said. CanTex Capital works with the city and neighborhoods before buying to ensure the impact aligns with the community's plan for its future. Advantages over traditional industrial, multifamily real estate Alex Sutterer, an executive vice president at NAI Hiffman, a Chicago-area commercial real estate firm, said that beyond being a place to store big equipment, IOS attracts investors for two main reasons: lower capital expenditure requirements than traditional industrial or multifamily properties and the potential for higher yields. "Capital improvements are also less specific to individual tenants, so owners can direct spending toward the property's overall functionality," Sutterer said. For private investors, IOS typically trades at a yield around one percentage point higher than traditional industrial properties, helping attract smaller investors and family offices. "We believe that gap will continue to narrow as more institutional capital enters this space," Sutterer added. Even for industrial properties with similar yields, he said the credit profile of tenants is generally stronger for IOS. Shallow-bay, multitenant industrial properties — industrial facilities that tend to be much smaller than big-box distribution warehouses — have comparable yields. But unlike the local businesses that tend to fill up shallow-bay sites, IOS tenants range from local businesses to those with investment-grade credit ratings, offering investors the potential for both yield and creditworthy tenants. And institutional money is making IOS more competitive. "Institutional capital has increased competition in IOS, and property values and lease rates have risen overall," Sutterer said. He added smaller investors can still find opportunities below institutional deal-size thresholds, although that does not mean every smaller deal is priced fairly. "We see opportunities to add value and earn yield in deals below $3 million–$5 million," Sutterer said. items.title: SpaceX Unveils $74B Data Center Plans In Texas, Arizona
items.description: SpaceX plans to spend $74B developing a pair of large-scale data center campuses in Arizona and Texas, marking a significant expansion of the Elon Musk -owned company’s digital infrastructure footprint. Wikimedia Commons/Gage Skidmore Elon Musk at a memorial service for slain conservative commentator Charlie Kirk The company announced the plans Thursday, outlining a $50B project at a new site in Cochise County, Arizona, and a $24B development on 444 acres near the firm’s headquarters in Starbase, Texas. The two campuses are taking different approaches to power. The Texas facility is planned to be powered by a natural gas power plant that SpaceX itself would develop, own and operate, Bloomberg reported . The Arizona campus, by contrast, would rely at least in part on gird electricity from local cooperatives. SpaceX has said the project will utilize existing renewable resources and cooling systems designed to avoid consuming groundwater — one of the most controversial elements of data center development in the desert Southwest. While SpaceX has been known as a commercial spaceflight company, Musk has increasingly repositioned the firm as an AI infrastructure provider for its own Grok models and outside hyperscale customers. The centerpiece of that shift was SpaceX’s February acquisition of Musk’s xAI in a $1.25T all-stock deal, merging the AI lab’s computing infrastructure into SpaceX’s launch and satellite business. SpaceX’s existing computing infrastructure is almost entirely concentrated in the Memphis, Tennessee, area at a pair of campuses called Colossus I and Colossus 2. The gigawatt-scale cluster has become a focal point for controversy , with environmental and civil rights groups alleging the company operated gas-powered generators to power its data centers without obtaining required Federal permits. Subsequent lawsuits from the NAACP and the Southern Environmental Law Center were opposed by the Trump administration, with the Justice Department asking a judge to dismiss the litigation on national security grounds. While Musk’s data center projects have courted controversy before, the timing of this week’s announcement is notable. It comes just over a week after voters across the U.S. delivered a sharp rebuke of data center development in numerous state and local elections in the industry’s most important markets. At the center of this shift was Texas, which has emerged as the country’s fastest-growing data center hub. Democrats scored upset victories across the state after campaigning in part on tighter oversight of data center development. Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated Republican incumbent Gov. Greg Abbott after making more restrictive data center policies a centerpiece of her campaign. The political shift occurred despite Musk reportedly spending roughly $180M supporting Republican candidates in Texas, including a $5M contribution to Abbott’s campaign. In the immediate aftermath of the election, Musk made clear that data center development was among the issues on his mind. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X. Arizona also faces the potential for more restrictive regulations on data centers following the midterms. Democrats claimed control over both chambers of the state legislature and retained the governor's office, with legislative Democrats openly discussing a potential pause on new data center development. Gov. Katie Hobbs , however, has said she is opposed to a blanket data center moratorium. Continue reading this story with a free account Log in or register Related Topics: Elon Musk , SpaceX

items.description: October 2026 Hottest Housing Markets By Hannah Jones Nov 13, 2026 Highlights Hartford-West Hartford-East Hartford, Conn. claimed the top spot in October for the first time since a summer run on top from May – July 2026. Buyer demand remains highly concentrated in the hottest markets, where listings attracted 2.6 times the national average number of views per property. The Midwest and Northeast were the only regions represented in the Top 20 for the 37th consecutive month. The list was evenly split this month, with 10 markets in the Midwest and 10 in the Northeast. Homes in the hottest markets moved significantly faster than the national norm, with median time on market of 37 days, more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm. Among large U.S. metros, Jacksonville, FL posted the biggest year-over-year improvement, jumping 70 spots to rank 189th nationally. The Hartford, CT metro moved up one spot from last month to claim the top spot on the hottest housing markets list for the first time since the summer. Hartford has ranked in the top 20 a total of 57 times, but has claimed the top spot only eight times. Located in New England, midway between Boston and New York, Hartford is an ideal landing spot for homebuyers looking to take advantage of the relatively low home prices in an otherwise pricey part of the country. In October, Hartford attracted 4.1 times the national average number of viewers per property. Homes sold in just 37 days, one day slower than a year ago but almost a month faster than the national norm. At a median listing price of $440,000, Hartford is priced just above the national norm, in a region generally priced well-above. Realtor.com’s Market Hotness rankings take into account two aspects of the housing market: 1) market demand, as measured by unique views per property on Realtor.com, and 2) the pace of the market as measured by the number of days a listing remains active on Realtor.com. ($549,000) is also priced below the regional norm. Connecticut accounts for four of the Top 20 markets, with Waterbury-Shelton, New Haven and Norwich joining Hartford at median list prices between $400,000 and $460,000. Springfield, Mass. and Rochester, N.Y. are priced below the national norm and well below the Northeast’s. New England’s compact geography is part of the draw. Hartford, New Haven, Waterbury and Springfield sit within roughly an hour’s drive of one another, so buyers can compare neighborhoods and price points across several metros without leaving the region. That flexibility concentrates demand, and inventory in these markets remains well below pre-pandemic norms. The pull shows up in buyer traffic, with all six New England markets on the list drawing at least 2.6 times the national average views per property, at or above the Top 20 average. For shoppers, widening the search within the region means more options but not much relief from competition, since the affordability that draws buyers to one market is drawing them to its neighbors as well. Jacksonville, Fla. led all large markets with the biggest ranking improvement, climbing 70 spots year over year, while San Francisco and Denver posted notable gains of 38 and 33 spots respectively. Riverside jumped 32 spots, and Sacramento rounded out the top five most improved, advancing 31 spots. The biggest movers were still fairly low on the overall list, ranging from 73rd for San Francisco to 216th for Denver. Four of the five biggest movers were located in the West, with three in California and one in the South. Though the South and West remain outside the nation's hottest markets, some areas are beginning to show growing demand and faster time-on-market. San Francisco stands out, with homes selling more than 3 weeks faster than the national norm, an acceleration likely boosted by the area’s ongoing AI boom . items.description: Download the full Q3 2026 Phoenix multifamily market report here.Highlights:Operating conditions in the Phoenix multifamily market improved during the third quarter, continuing patterns from the first half of this year. While property fundamentals have improved, investment activity has slowed in recent months.Vacancy dipped by 10 basis points in the third quarter, following steeper declines in the first half of the year. The current vacancy rate for stabilized properties is 6.5%, 70 basis points lower than levels from one year earlier.Area rents have gained ground in each of the first three quarters of 2026, although gains have been modest and current rents are still down slightly compared to one year ago. Rents ended the third quarter at $1,524 per month.Sales activity slowed in the third quarter, particularly among properties that have been delivered in recent years. The median price in sales that have closed to this point in 2026 is $229,600 per unit, while cap rates have averaged 6%.Phoenix multifamily market overviewThe Phoenix multifamily market has continued to record elevated levels of net absorption in 2026, which has combined with a slowing pace of new deliveries to support steady improvements in operating fundamentals. During the third quarter, net absorption reached more than 5,500 units, bringing the year-to-date total to approximately 18,000 units. This compares to net absorption of about 14,000 units during the first three quarters of 2025. The Goodyear/Avondale submarket has been a leading area for both demand growth and new supply. Net absorption in Goodyear/Avondale topped 1,000 units for the tenth consecutive quarter during the third quarter, and renter demand for units has been strongest in the West Valley. In the East Valley, absorption has been led by the Gilbert/Superstition Springs submarket to this point in 2026.Transaction activity slowed during the third quarter, after ticking higher in the prior three-month period. items.title: Zillow Rental Market Report: Demand for Single-Family Rentals Surges – RISmedia
items.description: Report: Demand Surges for Single-Family Rentals Single-family rental demand is rising nationwide, with demand up 24.3% year over year as the cost of homeownership continues to outpace renting. Home Agents November 12, 2026, 3 pm Reading Time: 3 mins read Zillow’s latest Rental Market Report shows that demand for renting single-family homes has risen, with consumers noting that they would need a $14,408 pay raise to cover the monthly costs of owning a home, even before saving for a down payment. Nationally, the typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, compared with $2,603 a month to own a single-family home with 20% down, or $360 more each month. “For a growing number of households, renting a house is a legitimate financial strategy,” said Kara Ng, senior economist at Zillow. “You get many of the lifestyle benefits, but it takes less income than owning and keeps more flexibility in the monthly budget. That’s the appeal for the deliberate renter.” The size of the raise depends on the market According to Zillow, the pay raise needed to buy is now the highest since early 2025, more than double the $6,463 it took in February 2026, when mortgage rates briefly fell below 6%. The gap looks very different from market to market. It’s largest in San Jose, where the income needed to buy ($404,925) is more than double the income needed to rent ($190,561), a gap of $214,364. The next largest gap is in San Francisco ($139,353), followed by San Diego ($84,101), New York ($78,208) and Los Angeles ($78,003). The smallest annual gaps are in Pittsburgh ($2,554), Houston ($4,500) and Cincinnati ($4,774). Buffalo is the only market where buying would not require a raise. Even with such a raise, would-be buyers still face another hurdle: saving a 20% down payment. About 30% of mortgage buyers use a gift or loan from family or friends, and 46% draw on two or more sources, including the use of down payment assistance programs , according to Zillow’s 2026 Consumer Housing Trends Report . In addition to the monthly cost, households deciding between renting and buying should weigh the upfront costs of buying, the chance to build equity and the opportunity for renters to invest their down payment instead. Zillow’s rent vs. buy research puts the national break-even timeline—the number of years a household would need to own before buying comes out ahead—at 7.8 years with 20% down. Rental demand keeps climbing As renting a house becomes an increasingly better value, more shoppers are turning to rentals. Rental demand is up 22.1% year over year nationwide, according to the Zillow Observed Renter Demand Index (ZORDI). Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for multifamily rentals. Rental demand surges in the Bay Area and the Sun Belt Demand rose the most in San Jose, where ZORDI is up 78.9% from a year ago, followed by San Francisco (60.5%), Austin (59.6%), Miami (51.5%) and Jacksonville (47.9%). San Jose and San Francisco are also among the markets where buying is furthest out of reach, and where rents are rising quickly, up 8.9% and 12.2% respectively. In Austin, Miami and Jacksonville, rent growth is more moderate, at 1.1%, 2.1% and 2.6%. Not every market is following the national trend. ZORDI is down year over year in Providence (-4.3%), Richmond (-1.9%), Baltimore (-1.7%), Hartford (-1.3%) and Washington, D.C. (-0.9%). For more information, visit www.zillow.com . items.description: Realpage Economy Express Episode 75 by Arben Skivjani Posted November 13, 2026 in Insights A surprisingly strong jobs report and stubborn inflation have all but settled the Fed's December decision, even as households and homebuyers keep feeling the squeeze. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the October jobs report showed 165,000 new jobs, almost three times what forecasters expected. Unemployment slipped to 4.1%, and paychecks grew 0.4% in a single month, the fastest pace since January. Job openings climbed to 7.5 million in September, more than expected, even though hiring remains slow. Consumer prices rose 0.4% in October and core prices were up 0.3% for the third month in a row, while the annual inflation rate could not be published because prices were never collected during last year's shutdown. Producer prices rose a calmer 0.3% in October after September's jump, but they are still up 6.5% from a year ago, the most since 2022. Fed funds futures pricing now treats a December rate hike as a sure thing, with some traders even betting on a half-point move. The University of Michigan's consumer survey found sentiment rose to 51, the best reading since August, while expected inflation eased to about 4.3%. Federal Reserve data show credit card balances grew in September at their fastest pace in nearly three years. Per the National Association of Realtors, existing home sales fell to their slowest pace since 2010, even with more homes for sale than at any point since 2019. items.description: Building Material Price Inflation Remains High Despite Energy Price Declines November 13, 2026 Jesse Wade No Comments The Producer Price Index for final demand was up 0.3% in October, after rising 1.4% in September. Compared to a year ago, final demand prices were up 6.5%. The price of goods used in new residential construction (including energy) was unchanged over the month and up 9.8% from last year, while the price of services was up 0.7% over the month and up 11.3% from last year. Combining goods and services, the price index for inputs to new residential construction was up 0.3% in October and 10.4% higher than last year. Input Goods The goods component has a larger importance to the inputs to residential construction price index, representing around 60% of the total. On a monthly basis, the price of input goods to new residential construction was unchanged in October after rising 1.7% in September. The input goods to residential construction index can be further broken down into two separate components, one measuring energy inputs with the other measuring remaining goods. The latter of these two components simply represents building materials used in residential construction, which makes up around 93% of the goods index. Energy input prices fell 3.3% in October and were 64.8% higher than a year ago. Building material prices were up 0.5% in October and up 5.8% compared to one year ago. Energy prices fell monthly as No. 2 diesel fuel prices fell 4.6% over the month but was a substantial 115.2% higher than a year ago. Outside of energy products, particleboard and fiberboard prices rose 5.4% over the month and were up 13.9% from a year ago. Softwood veneer and plywood prices were up 3.6% over the month and 24.5% higher than a year ago. Input Services Prices for service inputs to residential construction rose 0.7% in October. On a year-over-year basis, service input prices were up 11.3%. The price index for service inputs to residential construction can be broken out into three separate components: a trade services component, a transportation and warehousing services component, and a services excluding trade, transportation, and warehousing component (other services). The most significant component is trade services (around 60%), followed by other services (around 29%), and finally transportation and warehousing services (around 11%). The largest component, trade services, was up 13.2% from a year ago. The price of transportation and warehousing services has risen 24.6% from a year ago, while prices for other services were up 3.0% over the year. items.description: Why EAH Housing moved into Oregon to buy 1K affordable units The California-based developer acquired 19 properties from Catholic Charities of Oregon and opened a new affordable community in Sacramento. Published Nov. 13, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google Good Shepherd Village in Happy Valley, Oregon. Permission granted by EAH Housing Properties: 19 Buyer: EAH Housing Seller: Catholic Charities of Oregon Property type: Affordable Units: More than 1,000 Location: Oregon EAH Housing has built a large presence in California and Hawaii with more than 25,000 affordable homes across 240 properties. Earlier this week, the San Rafael, California-based nonprofit owner, manager and developer expanded north by purchasing more than 1,000 affordable homes in the Portland area from Catholic Charities of Oregon, according to a press release. The 19 properties, which include a mix of family, senior and supportive housing communities, are located in the Portland metro area, including Eugene, Sandy and Happy Valley. The acquisition represents the latest in a series of large affordable transitions over the past couple of years. “We view this acquisition as the beginning of a broader presence in Oregon and will continue exploring opportunities to expand our affordable housing portfolio across the state,” Katherine Fleming, EAH’s chief portfolio officer, told Multifamily Dive in emailed comments. “We are focused on identifying mission-aligned opportunities that support the long-term preservation and availability of affordable housing in high-need areas.” Oregon expansion Catholic Charities of Oregon was seeking a mission-aligned nonprofit partner committed to the long-term preservation of affordable housing and approached EAH, according to Fleming. “The acquisition represents a natural extension of the organization’s mission into the Pacific Northwest, where EAH Housing sees significant opportunities to address growing affordable housing needs,” Fleming said. While the acquisition allows EAH to continue preserving affordable housing, Catholic Charities will continue to provide supportive services to residents, according to the release. Guardian Real Estate Services will stay on as manager following the sale. Purchase and sale agreements are now in place for the transaction, which EAH and Catholic Charities have been working on since January 2026, per the release. Financial closings and property transfers are expected to occur on a rolling basis until the second quarter of 2027. Fleming said EAH is “evaluating opportunities for improvement across the properties to ensure they continue to provide high-quality affordable housing for Oregon residents for years to come.” Catholic Charities remains involved CEO of Catholic Charities Kaleen Deatherage said transitioning the properties to EAH Housing allowed them “to remain in the hands of a nonprofit deeply committed to affordable housing.” “Catholic Charities got into affordable housing to serve people,” Deatherage said in the release. “That purpose has not changed. What has changed is our understanding of where we can make the greatest impact.” Catholic Charities was represented by Jackson Ross of Newmark's Affordable Housing Advisors team. In addition to the Oregon acquisition, EAH also opened On Broadway, a new 140-unit affordable mixed-use housing community in Sacramento, according to a Nov. 13 news release shared with Multifamily Dive. The property, which includes one-, two- and three-bedroom apartments across two five-story buildings, serves individuals and families earning between 30% and 60% of the area median income. Thirty-seven homes are permanent supportive housing for individuals and families experiencing or at risk of homelessness. Major affordable deals The EAH Oregon acquisition is only the latest large affordable housing transaction in recent years. In May, nonprofit multifamily affordable housing investment manager National Equity Fund completed a massive deal acquiring National Affordable Housing Trust’s properties and fund management portfolio. In all, NEF is gaining 165 properties, encompassing 15,000 affordable homes nationwide, across 29 funds from NAHT. In December 2025, New York City-headquartered affordable housing preservation company Hudson Valley Property Group acquired a 22-property portfolio comprising 4,768 units across the western United States from Spokane, Washington-based Inland Group. In November 2024, New York City- and Los Angeles-based Standard Communities acquired a 100% affordable housing portfolio of over 6,000 apartment homes in more than 60 communities in four states. With the purchase of the portfolio, valued at over $1 billion, Standard entered Arizona, Colorado and Texas and grew its California portfolio to nearly 11,000 apartments. In May 2023, Chicago-based Nuveen acquired a portfolio of more than 12,000 units concentrated in New York City from New York City-based Omni Holding Co. This portfolio included several large apartment properties in the Bronx, Brooklyn and Queens, as well as buildings in Maryland, Massachusetts, Texas and other states. items.title: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance
items.description: Agencies extend comment period for proposed third-party risk management guidance Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Office of the Comptroller of the Currency National Credit Union Administration For release at 4:15 p.m. EST Share --> --> --> --> --> --> The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Federal Reserve Board, the National Credit Union Administration, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that they will extend, until December 16, the comment period for proposed guidance on managing risks associated with third-party relationships. Comments on the proposal were originally due November 16. The proposed guidance reflects the agencies' supervisory experience and lessons learned from examining financial institutions' third-party risk management practices. It is intended to help banks and credit unions tailor their risk management practices to the risks associated with individual third-party relationships. The proposed guidance takes a principles-based approach and, like all supervisory guidance, is non-binding. When finalized, the federal bank regulatory agencies plan to rescind existing third-party risk management guidance and replace it with the finalized guidance to promote consistency and prudent innovation in the banking industry. NCUA also plans to rescind its existing third-party risk management guidance and will conduct its own reviews to update related guidance as needed. Also today, the Federal Reserve Board separately announced that it will extend, until December 16, the comment period on a proposed third-party risk management guide specifically for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks. items.title: Existing-home sales miss estimates in October
items.description: Existing-home sales miss estimates in October by John Yellig November 13, 2026 Existing-home sales fell in October, missing already pessimistic estimates. Sales fell 5.5% month over month and 8.8% year over year to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million, the National Association of REALTORS® said in its monthly report. The consensus estimate was a rate of 3.87 million, down from 3.99 million in September. “Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023. As a result, home sales fell to their lowest level since August 2010,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.33% in October, up from 6.86% in September and 6.25% in October 2025, according to Freddie Mac. Regionally, sales declined in all four regions year over year, while they were down month over month in the Midwest, South and West and roughly flat in the Northeast. The median sales price rose 0.4% on an annual basis to $414,900, and inventory climbed 4.6% to 1.59 million homes. "For buyers, the monthly payment is often the biggest obstacle," Dallas-based REMAX DFW Associates agent Todd Luong said. "It is not just the price of the house. Buyers also have to consider property taxes, homeowners insurance, mortgage payments, maintenance and other expenses. … A buyer might qualify for a mortgage on paper but decide that the total monthly cost is simply too much." items.title: Atlanta’s housing market is entering a new phase. Here’s what comes next.
items.description: Atlanta’s housing market is entering a new phase. Here’s what comes next. by Atlanta Agent November 13, 2026 Anne Hartnett Hi, I'm Anne Hartnett and I am here with real estate economist Matthew Gardner to chat about our Q3 update. How are you, Matthew? Matthew Gardner I am well, Anne, how are you? Hartnett I'm great, thanks. So we've been waiting years for housing transactions to recover. At what point do we stop calling this a cyclical showdown and recognize that something more fundamental has changed in how Americans buy and sell homes? Gardner Great question. I mean, the short answer, as far as I'm concerned, is that we should have stopped calling it a cycle, or cyclical, about a year ago, because the forces that are holding sales down now aren't really the kind that are cycle-fixes. So let me explain. When existing home sales, we know, fell from over 6 million a year in 2021 to about 4 million in 2023, and they've been stuck there for nearly three years now. September numbers came in at 3.99 million. Now, there are three structural forces that explain this: One, the mortgage rate itself has become an asset that people just won't sell. I mean, in the second quarter, 49% of outstanding mortgages carried a rate at below 4%. Now, a record 43% were originated between mid-2019 and mid-2022. That means that selling gives up that loan — and that's not a cycle. It's a balance sheet decision, and it decays very slowly. There are some who suggest that the share of mortgages at 6% or higher, which is around 22.5% in Q2, only hits 27% to 29% by mid-2027. That's a slow grind. Now secondly, the buyer pool has aged. Last year, a typical first-time buyer was 40 years old, and a typical repeat buyer was 62. And last year, first-time buyers were 21% of purchases. That's a record low, and roughly half of their pre-2008 share. And a market that runs on equity rather than income, well, it transacts less often. And finally, the ten year Treasury, it's running around 5% today, and the 3% mortgage was a product of a zero-rate world that no reasonable forecast brings back. But this year, it gave us a small test of my belief. Briefly, back in February, mortgage rates dropped to below 6%, just. I think it was at the end of February. Lowest rate since 2022. But by June, they were back up to 6.5. Now they're above 7.3. Now, at that point, when they were very low, NAR had forecast a 14% jump in sales. But what are we doing today? We're running below last year. So the dip was far too brief to prove anything by itself. But in a normal cycle, cheaper money brings buyers back fast. This time it didn't. So the bottom line for me is that 6 million sales a year is the wrong benchmark. 2021 was an anomaly — a once-in-50-year financing, or refinancing, window. In 2019, we sold about 5.3 million existing homes. And my view is that the realistic norm, at least for the rest of this decade? Somewhere between 4 and 4.5 million. And we'll get there through life events such as job changes, divorce, death, downsizing, not through a rate rally. So for brokers, that changes their business model. In a 4 million-unit market, well, the pipeline isn't buyers waiting for rates to fall. It's people who have to move regardless of rate — relocations, estate sales, divorces, retirees. Now those transactions happen at 7%. If your marketing is built around a quote, wait for rates to drop, unquote, well, you're building for a market, unfortunately, that may not show up. Hartnett Housing drives everything from construction and lending to consumer spending. Could several years of depressed transaction volume begin to weigh on broader economic growth? Gardner It already has, but interestingly, not in the way that most people assume. So let's start with what counts. The sale of an existing home is just a transfer of an asset. It doesn't add to GDP or growth. What counts is construction, remodeling and also the services around a transaction — that would be brokerage commissions, and also households buying new furniture, new appliances, that follow any move. Residential investment is only 3.7% of GDP against a historic average of about five. Now, housing’s total share of the economy? About 16%. That's actually still the lowest we've seen since 2019. Now, residential investment shrank for five straight quarters, falling at an annual rate of about 7.8% in Q1. It did tick up a bit in the second quarter. So no doubt housing has been a drag. But the contrarian part is that the economy grew right through it. Nonresidential investment rose 8.5% in the second quarter, driven by AI equipment and also software. Consumer spending rose 3.4%. You see, homeowners are sitting on substantial equity, and that wealth supports spending even when they don't move. Low transactional volumes is a slow leak, not a recession trigger. Now the real risk, as I see it, is actually different. Housing's historically been the economy's shock absorber. A recession hits the Fed cuts rates to stimulate the economy, ultimately mortgage rates drop, housing turns and construction hiring leads to a recovery. Now that channel’s impaired. Ten-year treasury near five, inflation at 3.4, and in early October, markets are still weighing whether the Fed's next move could be to hike in order to address inflation. But if the labor market weakens further — now remember, September we added just 29000 jobs — well, the Fed should be cutting rates, but I just don't see that happening. So we may not get the usual housing-led rebound on the other side. Now where you feel the drag first is local and also sectoral. It's not in GDP. It shows up in title, escrow, mortgage originations, moving companies, furniture retailers and obviously broker incomes, but also shows up in city and state budgets. Columbia Senior Attorney - Arizona or New Mexico Explore More Job Openings U.S. Treasury’s Proposed Regulations Concerning Title X Of The 21st Century ROAD To Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know by: John Cagigas , Winstead - News Alert Monday, November 9, 2026 Related Practices & Jurisdictions Real Estate Financial Institutions Banking Administrative Regulatory All Federal Print Mail Download />i Introduction On July 11, 2026, the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 19521 (the “ Act ”). As discussed in our June 24 article, “Title X of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act: What Real Estate Developers, Investors and Lenders Need to Know” (the “ Initial Article ”), Title X of the Act generally bars a “ large institutional investor ” from buying—or entering into a contract to buy—a “ single-family home ” unless a statutory exception applies. Under the Act, a covered investor must be a qualifying for-profit entity engaged in the single-family rental (“ SFR ”) business that, alone or with others acting “ in concert ,” has direct or indirect “ investment control ” over at least 350 single-family homes. Homes acquired through statutory exceptions after July 11, 2026, are excluded from that count. For this purpose, a “ single-family home ” generally means a structure with no more than two dwelling units, excluding manufactured homes. On October 23, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury (the “ Treasury ”) issued proposed regulations under Title X (proposed 31 C.F.R. Part 36, the “ Proposed Regulations ”). The Proposed Regulations explain several exceptions for build-to-rent (“ BTR ”), renovate-to-rent, homeownership programs, creditor enforcement and institutional resales, as well as rules affecting investment funds and managers. However, some of the Treasury’s proposals could also complicate common BTR development and sale structures. As of the date hereof, the Proposed Regulations are not binding or final, and the Treasury expects additional rulemakings. Public comments on the Proposed Regulations will be due by November 23, 2026, and the statutory purchase prohibition under the Act becomes effective January 7, 2027, independent of when final regulations are adopted. Key Takeaways The headline for BTR is mixed: the Treasury proposes a purchase deadline of 18 months after a home receives its certificate of occupancy, but also confirms that qualifying homes can be resold repeatedly between covered institutional investors. The Treasury also proposes a written-program requirement for several exceptions and a more detailed test for passive investors. Important gaps remain that are unresolved in the Proposed Regulations, including how the Act applies to fund aggregation, equity transfers, pre-effective-date purchase contracts and BTR homes leased before an institutional sale. The discussion below distinguishes what Congress expressly provided in the Act from the additional conditions the Treasury now offers in the in the Proposed Regulations. BTR Protection: Greater Certainty, but a Narrower Initial Acquisition Window The Act expressly allows purchases under a BTR program in which a large institutional investor “ purchases, constructs, or constructs and retains ” newly constructed homes to be managed as rentals. Our Initial Article explained why that language appeared to protect traditional BTR development and institutional takeout sales. The Treasury’s proposed definition, however, focuses on when a home is purchased and how it is first occupied. Proposed § 36.5 would require a home acquired under the BTR exception to (i) have no previous owner-occupant, (ii) be purchased within 18 months after its certificate of occupancy (or local equivalent), and (iii) be first occupied by renters after the purchase. The Treasury rejected an alternative that would treat an older home as “ newly constructed ” solely because it was originally built and continuously used as a rental. The proposal does not separately explain how these purchase-focused requirements apply when an institutional investor itself constructs and retains the homes, a scenario the Act expressly includes. This may matter for merchant-builders that deliver a community in phases, lease homes as they are completed and sell the stabilized project in one transaction. Because the proposed deadline is tied to each home’s certificate of occupancy, earlier phases could fall outside the proposed BTR exception even while later phases qualify. The Treasury has not proposed a project-wide extension measured from the final phase or stabilization. Another statutory exception may be needed for homes that miss the 18-month window. A second issue concerns lease-up before closing. The proposed § 36.5(c) states that homes must be “ after the purchase, first occupied by renters .” That language appears to require that first-time rental occupancy occur after the institutional buyer purchases the homes, so a home already renter-occupied before sale would appear ineligible for this exception. The Proposed Regulations do not expressly disqualify pre-leased homes or analyze pre-sale lease-up, so clarification remains warranted before buyers rely on this exception. The Act permits BTR homes in both entirely rental and mixed rental/owner-occupied communities, and the Treasury confirms that the exception is not lost simply because a development also contains other property types. The rule still applies home-by-home: conventional apartment buildings with three or more dwelling units per structure generally fall outside the Act’s definition of “ single-family home ,” while qualifying SFR homes within the same development remain subject to the applicable exception. items.title: The seasonal decline in housing inventory is in full force
items.description: Housing inventory Housing inventory has picked up recently, after mortgage rates went above 6.64% and then shot up toward 7.60%. Inventory growth had been very tame this year, with some weeks negative year over year. As housing inventory returns to normal levels, it takes weaker demand to get stronger growth and rates moving toward 7.60% did that. Still, it's more about sales taking longer to happen and demand being hit, because new listings data didn’t budge much recently. Now, we are in the full-blown seasonal decline as we get ready to prep for spring 2027. Inventory growth is running at 7.11% over last year even with easier comps, as last year demand was running toward a 9-month high in December of 2025. Weekly inventory change (Nov. 6-Nov. 13): Inventory fell from 902,740 to 895,988 Same week last year (Nov. 7-Nov. 14): Inventory fell from 842,257 to 836,487 New listings New listings have been in their seasonal decline since June and nothing abnormal with this data line has happened in 2026; in fact, it’s been the best year of new listings since 2022. One concern I had about higher rates is that more people might simply not list their homes — as they did in the second half of 2022 due to higher rates. However, that hasn’t happened; we did see a more noticeable year-over-year decline this last week, but for the most part it’s been a healthy year. In a normal environment, new listings range from 80,000 to 100,000 per week during peak periods. For context, during the housing bubble years, new listings ranged from 250,000 to 400,000 per week for several years . Here is last week’s new listings data for the past two years: 2026: 53,162 2025: 56,569 Price-cut percentage Typically, about one-third of homes see price reductions before they sell, reflecting the housing market’s dynamic nature. Overall, price-cut percentages this year have been lower than last year. This held true until rates moved above 6.64% and then above 7%. At that point demand fell and the year-over-year price-cut percentage rose 1%. In my 2026 home-price forecast, I called for a national decline of -0.62% for the year. Home-price growth really isn’t going anywhere this year and my -0.62% forecast may be hard to achieve, since most home-price indices show growth between 1% and 2%. However, with higher rates and a rising price-cut percentage, we will be closer to the forecast. Clearly, if rates hadn’t risen above 6.75%, pricing data wouldn’t have shown the recent slowdown. The price-cut percentage for last week: 2026: 43.% 2025: 42% 10-year yield and mortgage rates In the 2026 HousingWire forecast , I anticipated the following ranges: Mortgage rates between 5.75% and 6.75% The 10-year yield fluctuating between 3.80% and 4.60% Last week wasn’t good for mortgage rates or the bond market: we had hawkish Fed statements and hot inflation data. We were getting closer to mortgage rates below 7% for the holidays, but they made a big reversal from 7.17% to 7.50%. In addition, President Trump talked about raising tariffs against Mexico and we still have no deal with Iran. Pretty much everything you needed for rates to go lower went the other way — something I talked about in this episode of the HousingWire Daily podcast with Editor in Chief Sarah Wheeler. Mortgage spreads Mortgage spreads have worsened recently, but they did improve last week. Traditionally, when mortgage rates escalate with the 10-year yield and then make a big reversal — like we just had from a 5.35% 10-year yield top that dropped down toward 4.82% — spreads do get worse to try to compress mortgage rate volatility. items.title: Apartment rents diverge: San Francisco rises, the Sun Belt falls
items.description: America's apartment landscape has become a tale of two opposing rent trends. Rents are climbing in the Bay Area and the Midwest, while much of the Sun Belt is still sliding. National same-store asking rents edged up 1.7% from a year earlier in October, the biggest annual gain since May 2023, apartment industry data firm RealPage reported Nov. 11. The national figure hides a wide gap. San Francisco rents jumped 14.7%, evidence of why city officials are pressing the supply button to drive housing construction. San Antonio rents dropped 2.6%. The month-over-month picture illustrates less dramatic change. RealPage showed that rents fell 0.7% in October, the first monthly cut of 2026. The company said the annual gain came less from strong pricing than from weak months dropping out of the calculation, making for stronger year-over-year comparables. Other trackers show the same upward drift, with different monthly readings. Yardi Matrix reported rents up 0.1% in October, with annual growth of 1.4%, the strongest in more than three years. Apartments.com put annual growth at 1.6%, even as rents slipped 0.15% for the month. Supply wave cools Supply and demand are edging toward balance. RealPage said renters absorbed nearly 304,800 conventional apartments in the year ending in Q3 2026. Developers completed nearly 318,000 units over the same period, almost half the late-2024 peak. Occupancy eased to 95%, down 20 basis points from September. It is still up 40 basis points this year and 10 basis points above October 2025. Landlords hit the brakes Improving rents haven't translated into a property buying spree. Camden Property Trust , a large apartment landlord, walked away from two acquisitions and canceled two planned development projects. The Federal Reserve's rate hike was a main reason, rental economist Jay Parsons wrote on LinkedIn. Two deals under contract fell through after the hike, Camden CEO Alex Jessett said on the third-quarter earnings call. Camden asked for lower prices, and the sellers declined. Buying also beat building on cost. Camden bought an asset at about $370,000 a door, while building it would have cost north of $600,000, Jessett said. Camden's earnings show an unevenly improving market. Funds from operations, a standard earnings measure for real estate investment trusts, were $1.70 per diluted share in the third quarter. Core funds from operations were $1.71, $0.02 above the company's guidance midpoint. "A higher-for-longer rate environment may equate to a lower-for-longer supply environment," Parsons wrote. Fewer projects penciling out means fewer new apartment options for renters. Coasts and Midwest lead Northern California took the top three spots for rent power among the 50 largest markets, RealPage said. San Francisco rose 14.7%, San Jose 9.5% and Oakland 8.5%. All three are running near 97% occupancy. Midwest metros fill much of the rest of the top 10. Milwaukee led at 4.2%, followed by Chicago at 3.3%, and Kansas City and Cleveland at 3.1% each. Detroit and St. Louis each gained 2.7% and just missed the cut. Sun Belt still lags Most Sun Belt and Florida markets continued to decline. The South as a region returned to annual growth, but only by 0.5%. San Antonio had the deepest decline in rents among big markets at 2.6%. Its occupancy of 92.5% was the lowest of the 50 largest markets. Houston fell 1.8%, followed by drops in Tampa of 1%, Charlotte of 0.9% and Denver of 0.8%. Several Sun Belt markets have turned the corner, however. Jacksonville rose 2.6%, Raleigh 1.0%, Atlanta 0.8%, Austin and Miami 0.6% each, and Phoenix 0.4%. items.title: Renewals Carry Apartment REIT Pricing as Coastal and Sun Belt Results Split
items.description: Renewals Carry Apartment REIT Pricing as Coastal and Sun Belt Results Split by Meggan Taylor Posted November 12, 2026 in REIT Renewals and low turnover continued to support apartment REIT pricing in 3rd quarter 2026, while new lease performance remained pressured across much of the Sun Belt. Results from Camden Property Trust, Essex Property Trust, Mid-America Apartment Communities (MAA), UDR and Vivmark Residential highlighted a sharp divide between coastal and Sun Belt markets, as coastal-heavy operators raised guidance and Sun Belt-focused peers lowered expectations. A merger and major portfolio shifts reshaped the group Vivmark Residential reported its first quarterly results since AvalonBay Communities and Equity Residential completed their merger on Aug. 17, creating a same-store portfolio of 157,377 apartment homes. The company raised its target for yearly cost savings and revenue gains from the combination by $10 million to $135 million. COO Michael Manelis said years of separate operations gave Vivmark “a multi-year A/B test,” letting it compare the two companies’ practices and keep what works best. Other operators also changed their portfolio exposure. Camden completed the roughly $1.6 billion sale of 11 California communities on July 29, and UDR formed a $2 billion partnership with Apollo, covering 19 communities. As a result, three of the five REITs now operate meaningfully different portfolios than a year ago. Renewals continued to carry lease pricing Renewals remained the primary source of pricing strength. Renewal lease rates rose 5.3% at Essex, MAA and Vivmark and 3.6% at Camden, while retention remained elevated across portfolios. UDR reported a record-high 3rd quarter retention rate of 52%, and MAA recorded a record-low share (10.1%) of move-outs to homeownership. Management tied that stability largely to housing costs. “We see sustained high homeownership costs, and we see residents continuing to stay in place, both for cyclical and structural reasons,” UDR CFO Dave Bragg said. MAA added that the dollar gap between new and renewal rents has held at about $190 to $200 for four quarters, a small difference next to the cost and hassle of moving. New lease pricing stayed negative as concessions persisted New lease pricing told a different story. New lease rates declined at four of the five REITs, ranging from -6.0% at MAA to -0.2% at Essex. Vivmark was the only exception, with new lease rates up 0.4%. Camden and MAA attributed the weakness largely to lease-up discounting and lease mix. “Concessions have remained remarkably sticky, seemingly led by many merchant builders now turned reluctant operators,” Camden CEO Alex Jessett said. MAA said its year-to-date new lease decline narrows to -1.9% when the departing resident stayed only one lease term, a figure it views as a better gauge of market rents. Northern California and Denver marked the extremes Regional performance diverged sharply. Northern California led results at both Vivmark and Essex, where same-store NOI rose 11.2% and 7.0%, respectively. At UDR, new lease rates rose 5.7% in the West region but fell 7.2% in the Southwest region. Denver sat at the other end, with same-store NOI down 9.6% at Vivmark and nearly 7% at both Camden and MAA. Essex linked Northern California’s strength to limited supply and rents that remain below historical norms relative to incomes. By its estimate, rents could rise more than 20%, assuming no wage growth, before rent-to-income ratios returned to pre-COVID levels. Meanwhile, Camden tied most of its Denver revenue decline to local legislation that stopped it from billing residents for common-area utilities, on top of persistent concessions. Guidance split along portfolio lines Full-year outlooks followed the same divide. Essex, UDR and Vivmark raised same-store revenue guidance, while Camden and MAA lowered theirs. Both Sun Belt-focused REITs cited timing: MAA said new lease pricing is recovering later than expected, and Camden said September was softer than expected. Both still pointed to early improvement as supply eases. “October new resident lease pricing improved from September, counter to the normal seasonal pattern,” MAA CEO Brad Hill said. What to watch in 4th quarter The key question for 4th quarter is whether easing supply translates into firmer revenue growth in Sun Belt markets. With completions declining and demand holding up, those results should show whether supply-heavy markets are beginning to close the gap with coastal markets. items.description: NMHC and RETTC say Democrats have won both chambers, producing divided government, and argue housing costs are the issue candidates in both parties campaigned on. About 20% of the 120th Congress will be new, which the groups see as a chance to educate lawmakers on supply, permitting and technology that can cut costs. The apartment industry wants Congress to build on the ROAD to Housing Act and favors a balanced approach to affordability measures that avoids driving up costs. Key Takeaways Apartment industry leaders say housing affordability is the issue most likely to unite Washington after the midterms, according to a post from the National Multifamily Housing Council. NMHC President Sharon Wilson Géno and Kevin Donnelly, executive director and chief advocacy officer of its RETTC affiliate, wrote that Democrats have taken both chambers of Congress, with some races still being counted. Instead, they favor balanced measures that protect residents and support innovation without driving up rental costs. NMHC wants to shape those discussions early. Its priorities also align with developers seeking faster permitting and fewer cost mandates. items.title: No Relief: Credit Conditions for Builders Still Tightening
items.description: No Relief: Credit Conditions for Builders Still Tightening November 13, 2026 Paul Emrath No Comments Credit conditions on loans for residential Land Acquisition, Development & Construction (AD&C) were still tightening in the third quarter of 2026, according to NAHB’s quarterly survey on AD&C Financing. The net easing index derived from the survey posted a third-quarter reading of -15.3 (the negative number indicating net tightening). This marks the nineteenth consecutive quarter during which residential builders and developers have reported tightening credit conditions. The NAHB survey agrees closely with the third-quarter results reported by lenders in the Federal Reserve’s survey of senior loan officers, as the net easing index constructed from the Fed survey posted a third-quarter reading of -15.5. Although lenders previously reported a slight easing in 2026 Q2, lenders have generally agreed with builders and developers that credit conditions have been tightening since the beginning of 2022. The Fed survey’s net easing index was in negative territory (indicating net tightening) for 18 of the past 19 quarters. More details from the Fed’s survey of lenders—including measures of demand and net easing for residential mortgages—appeared in a previous post . Meanwhile, measures on the cost of AD&C credit exhibited a combination of relatively small quarter-to-quarter changes, signaling no clear trend in either direction. The average contract interest rate declined from 8.09% in the second quarter to 7.83% in the third quarter on loans for land development, but increased for the other three categories of loans tracked in the NAHB AD&C survey: from 7.77% to 8.08% on loans for land acquisition, from 7.28% to 7.72% on loans for speculative single-family construction, and from 7.01% to 7.27% on loans for pre-sold single-family construction. However, the initial points charged by lenders declined on all four categories of AD&C loans in the third quarter: from 1.05% to 0.86% on loans for land acquisition, from 1.05% to 0.97% on loans for land development, from 0.85% to 0.71% on loans for speculative single-family construction, and from 0.71% to 0.51% on loans for pre-sold single-family construction. Those changes left the average effective interest rate (taking both contract rate and initial points into account) essentially unchanged at 11.83% (compared 11.82% in the second quarter) on loans for speculative single-family construction. The average effective rate increased from 10.43% to 10.55% on loans for land acquisition, but declined from 12.59% to 11.69% on loans for land development, and from 11.67% to 11.47% on loans for pre-sold single-family construction. The NAHB AD&C survey also revealed that 32% of respondents who built single-family homes during the third quarter of 2026 financed some of their homes with a construction-to-permanent (one-time-close) loan made to the ultimate home buyer. On average, 58% of the homes these respondents built were financed in this manner. While the market for residential mortgages has been showing signs of stress recently—including a recent decline in mortgage applications and increase in delinquencies —it is important not to overlook the role access to AD&C credit plays in helping builders and developers expand the supply of affordable housing. More detail on credit conditions for residential builders and developers is available on NAHB’s AD&C Financing Survey web page . items.title: Members Of Congress Have Questions For Brookfield After Its Mass Mobile Home Purchase
items.description: Brookfield quietly closed on the acquisition of the largest privately held manufactured housing portfolio in the United States this year, prompting some members of Congress to inquire about the investment giant’s plans for the properties it now owns. Bisnow/Ethan Rothstein Brookfield purchased Yes Communities from GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, in the second quarter, public filings and statements from Brookfield management indicate. Brookfield hasn’t publicized its acquisition of the Denver-based operator of nearly 300 manufactured home developments, but three Democrats from the House of Representatives nonetheless sent a letter to the firm last month voicing concern about the purchase and seeking pledges for tenant protections. Reps. Maxwell Alejandro Frost, Gabe Vasquez and Rashida Tlaib asked management at New York-based Brookfield Asset Management, the publicly traded arm of Toronto-based Brookfield, and Brookfield Real Estate Group to provide assurances that residents’ quality of life wouldn’t be impacted by the deal. The representatives gave BAM until Nov. 20 to respond. The asset management giant hadn’t yet replied as of mid-November, Frost’s office confirmed to Bisnow on Nov. 9. Brookfield didn’t respond to multiple requests for comment. It hasn’t formally announced the acquisition, which was first rumored to be in the works in September 2025, but BAM said in second-quarter filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission that it acquired “the largest privately held U.S. manufactured home portfolio.” Yes Communities operates more than 55,000 housing sites across the U.S., with a focus on the Southwest, Midwest and Southeast. A purchase price for the portfolio is unknown, but BAM said it spent $5.2B in the second quarter on its real estate business, including the manufactured home portfolio and the take-private of an industrial outdoor storage portfolio. Brookfield announced a $1.2B all-cash deal in February to buy Peakstone Realty Trust, a REIT with 60 IOS properties and 16 traditional industrial assets. In its second-quarter filings, Brookfield Real Estate Income Trust disclosed a new investment in a 2% ownership interest in 294 manufactured housing properties at a book value of $86.6M, which aligns with the number of properties under the Yes Communities banner. BAM Chief Financial Officer Hadley Peer Marshall also disclosed on the second-quarter earnings call that a Brookfield fund had made its first investment by deploying capital to Yes Communities. Other affiliates of Brookfield may have also contributed capital for the Yes Communities acquisition. Brookfield REIT said in an investor presentation on its website that as of Sept. 30, it owned a 294-community manufactured housing portfolio across 23 states, the same number of states Yes Communities is active in. Wikimedia Commons; Office of Maxwell Frost Democratic Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Gabriel Vasquez and Maxwell Frost have asked Brookfield about its acquisition of Yes Communities. Executives from Brookfield held one virtual meeting with residents and their advocates following the acquisition that was facilitated by the Private Equity Stakeholder Project and MHAction, two nonprofit advocacy groups, PESP confirmed to Bisnow . GIC and another unnamed institutional investor acquired a 71% equity interest in Yes Communities in 2016, with Stockbridge Capital Group holding on to the remaining stake. Brookfield was reportedly in talks with GIC about acquiring its stake for more than $10B, and it is unclear exactly the size of Brookfield's interest in Yes Communities or how much it paid. In their letter from Oct. 13, the three members of Congress sought details about the acquisition. The letter outlines previous tenants' complaints with Yes Communities for high rent increases, excessive fees and neglect of routine maintenance and says that Brookfield “has the opportunity to change this scenario” and “support meaningful protections for its residents.” “Given the challenges our constituents have experienced at Yes! properties, as well as broader concerns about the private equity business model, we seek assurances that Brookfield will prioritize improving residents’ quality of life and protecting their economic and housing stability, rather than exacerbating the economic challenges they already face,” the representatives wrote. The letter specifically asks Brookfield to disclose whether it plans to increase rents by more than 3% annually, to outline its policy regarding new and existing fees, and to confirm whether it will refrain from serial eviction filings for routine rent collection. The letter asks BAM to commit to meet regularly with tenants and to cooperate with tenant groups that are seeking to collectively purchase their communities. The housing legislation that made it to the president’s desk includes new restrictions on existing home purchases from institutional investors but carves out broad exemptions for new development of single-family communities built as rentals. items.title: MAG Partners Taps Former Swire Exec For Miami Debut
items.description: After four years as senior vice president of development at Swire Properties , Kevin Davenport is joining MaryAnne Gilmartin 's team to lead her Manhattan-based firm's South Florida expansion. Courtesy of MAG Partners Kevin Davenport previously worked at Swire Properties and BGRE, formerly Brookfield Properties. MAG Partners named Davenport the senior vice president and head of development of South Florida, according to a release. The company is also looking to lease office space in Downtown Miami, reported Commercial Observer, which first reported the announcement . "Miami has grown into a global city, with the capital, talent and demand to support large, complex, mixed-use projects," MAG Partners wrote in a LinkedIn post on Thursday . "The projects that will define the region are being built now, and they depend on strong partnerships and teams that know how to deliver at scale. That is the work we do." The new role comes after MAG sought to hire a seasoned development executive to head a mixed-use tower with a hotel, luxury condos and retail spanning more than 1M SF at the beginning of this year. It is unclear where MAG is in the process of the unnamed project. MAG Partners declined to disclose any details about its Miami office lease and the project. Davenport's recent work with Swire included leading the development of the 2.7M SF Residences at Mandarin Oriental , Miami, which broke ground last month . He also led the predevelopment of Swire's planned 1.7M SF One Brickell City Centre office project before it was canceled and the site was sold to The Melo Group last year. Before Swire, Davenport spent 10 years at Brookfield Properties , which rebranded to BGRE in July, and held positions at Hines and the Blackstone Group , according to his LinkedIn. “MaryAnne and the MAG Partners team share my development ethos: a commitment to great design, thoughtful execution and creating places that have a lasting impact,” Davenport said in a statement. “I’m excited to build the company’s presence in South Florida.” This will be MAG Partners' first known venture into South Florida, according to its website. Gilmartin spearheaded the development of the Barclays Center basketball arena while working as an executive with Forest City Ratner before she was named CEO in 2013. After more than two decades with the company, she stepped down from her role and founded MAG Partners in 2018. MAG Partners has designed, built and operated more than 16M SF of office, residential and mixed-use projects with a total value of more than $10B, according to the release. items.title: How Training Veterans in Skilled Trades Could Speed Up Homebuilding and Ease Housing Costs
items.description: A severe shortage of skilled workers entering the residential construction sector has had a major impact on affordability, but the Home Builders Institute (HBI) believes the country’s large veteran population may be part of the solution. The skilled labor shortage has led to an increase in construction time, with each home taking nearly two months longer to build, according to an HBI study . Due to the delays, there was a reduction of 19,000 homes built in 2024, representing an economic loss of over $8 billion, the study found. Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC) estimated that the construction industry needs to attract roughly 349,000 net new workers in 2026 and 456,000 new workers in 2027 to meet demand for construction services. There are a number of factors in the past 30 years that have led to the labor shortage, according to HBI CEO Ed Brady . First, a strong push for four-year degrees led many young people toward academic careers rather than trades. With more people retiring from the workforce than entering, the shortage began. The issue was compounded during the financial crisis of 2008, when the residential construction field lost tons of skilled workers because there wasn’t enough work. Without enough housing construction, workers left for jobs in manufacturing and hospitality or retired early, according to Brady. More recently, rocky immigration policies have challenged the skilled labor workforce, Brady explains. When finding a solution to the shortage became dire, HBI believed that the veteran and transitioning military population was “an untapped market.” The result was the HBI Military Services Program, which trains veterans, transitioning military service members, and their dependents in skilled trades. On Monday, HBI and Invitation Homes announced a new partnership that will continue HBI’s mission to create opportunities for transitioning military service members, veterans, and their families. The partnership includes an unspecified investment from Invitation Homes in HBI’s Military Services Program. It will also open doors for former military service members who complete HBI training to access job opportunities with the premier leasing and management company. For nearly a decade, HBI has been raising awareness of the benefits of a career in a skilled trade among former members. It has proceeded to train, certify, and assist veterans and their families in finding successful careers. HBI’s Military Services Program was supported early on by major companies like The Home Depot Foundation and Dewalt. It was recently given a $1 million gift from Google.org , and now Invitation Homes has joined the worthy cause. These vital investments help HBI reach even more service members on their mission, according to Brady. “It provides scale. We’re not changing our model—we feel like our model works. We introduce them to the industry, we train them in the industry, we certify them, we connect them to the industry to get a job,” Brady tells Realtor.com® . “But the dollars from Invitation Homes, the dollars that Google have given us to apply into the veteran space just gives us more scale. We can provide better service, and we can grow our programs to serve more veterans, more transitioning military, even the spouses of veterans.” Loading... (Stock image) Bloomberg via Getty Images Expanding training programs for former military could make a huge difference in the skilled labor shortage being experienced by residential construction. “In many cases, the demographic of soldiers that want to be outside, want to work with their hands, and have that physicality, it’s natural for them to look at our industry,” says Brady. “They’ve got more discipline, they know how to create a task and how to do a job. They have a desire to be productive and build a career.” Brady has also observed that many veterans want to “control their own destiny” once they leave the military. The desire to not be dependent on anyone else or an organization makes them great candidates for entrepreneurship, business ownership, and contracting roles.
