items.title: Reverse mortgage executives read the tea leaves to decipher the industry's next chapter
items.description: At this week's National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Convention & Expo in San Antonio, executives offered their thoughts on the evolving product landscape and efforts to expand the sales force while cautioning that hurdles around consumer misperceptions remain. In a panel discussion held Tuesday and moderated by former NRMLA board member and current Texas Mortgage Bankers Association CEO Scott Norman , executives covered a wide range of topics including proprietary reverse mortgages , distribution efforts with traditional forward lenders and the potential for a broad marketing push to consumers. "I think one of the things that's held us back is our lack of distribution," said Jim Cory , managing director of Guild Mortgage 's reverse division. "It's such a sea change in our business to suddenly have to go from this beloved group that we have here and begin adding to it. And literally thousands of loan originators now have access to this product." Proprietary products push the envelope At a time when federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs) have dropped to their lowest levels in about 10 years , private-label loans have stepped up to fill the void. Data compiled by New View Advisors showed that proprietary products accounted for 60% of all reverse mortgage volume in September 2026 — a share that is expected to continue growing. Melissa Macerato , the newly appointed president and chief commercial officer at Longbridge Financial , said that these products have changed business for the better and that the industry would "be in a very different place" without them. Longbridge has been among the lenders to introduce private-label solutions in recent years through its Platinum suite and HELOC for Seniors . Macerato said she expects to see more hybrid reverse mortgage products developed soon, with a focus on giving borrowers higher proceeds alongside mandatory but flexible payments. "In order to get that broader distribution, in order to have more exposure for our products, we're going to have to start speaking the language and developing products that more mainstream mortgage entities and loan officers really understand," she said. Jonathan Scarpati , chief production officer at Finance of America , told NRMLA attendees that the products "from 10 years ago are not reverse mortgages that everyone is selling today." His company has also been at the forefront of product innovation with its HomeSafe suite — including a second-lien option that allows borrowers to tap into their home equity without touching their low-rate first mortgage. But Scarpati believes that new products are meant to "cast a wider net" rather than replace the traditional HECM that's been the industry's cornerstone since the program was authorized in 1987. Mike Kent , senior vice president of corporate development and industry relations at Onity Mortgage , agreed. "The reason we have proprietary products is that [the HECM] set the baseline, it set the standards, it ushered in the appropriate regulation and safeguards for the product, and it kind of cleared the way for us to begin to innovate," Kent said. Scarpati also pushed back against the notion that more competition in reverse mortgages is a bad thing. "I think 2027 is a very pivotal moment for the industry in general," he said. "I think as the products continue to evolve, some of them are looking closer to the forward industry. … The closer we have our products look to what the forward industry is used to, the more growth and the more adoption we're going to get." Forward lenders could open their doors wider Cory said that lack of distribution has been a longstanding obstacle for the industry. But many of the large independent mortgage banks ( IMBs ) — including Guild, Rate , Fairway Home Mortgage and CrossCountry Mortgage — now have a visible presence in the space. According to Cory, the six largest IMBs have about 17,000 originators today, and business would expand significantly if this group alone put more resources into reverse. Jesse Allen , president of the 55+ lending division at Rate, said that while the largest IMBs have reverse mortgage options to offer borrowers, the ongoing hurdle is to get more engagement from loan officers. That work falls to reverse specialists, who must do a better job of sharing their knowledge and building relationships. "If you want other people to trust you, you have to really know your craft," Allen said. "Language matters. And so, as a reverse industry, I would encourage all of you to think about the language you use when you walk in with a traditional mortgage loan officer and a real estate agent. Use language that feels familiar to them and that will start to build trust." Some companies are introducing technology solutions to engage LOs who are unfamiliar with reverse products. Earlier this month, Nationwide Equities Corp. launched ReverseReach , a tool to help uncover reverse mortgage opportunities in existing customer databases and referral networks. And in July, Reverse Market Insight expanded its loan qualification tool to include Smartfi Home Loans ' proprietary products, part of Smartfi's push to get more traditional LOs involved. Scarpati said many lenders are looking for new opportunities as traditional purchase and refinance is expected to decline in 2027 . Home equity lending, including reverse mortgages, presents a massive opportunity as U.S. homeowners hold roughly $35 trillion in equity , including $15 trillion among those 62 and older. "I've been in locales that are super beautiful, well organized, great facilities, but they lacked a personality ... I've never been able to replicate the feeling that Budapest holds anywhere else," she said. EU citizens can work remotely from Hungary long-term if they meet certain requirements, while Hungary's White Card scheme, which provides one- or two-year residency permits for digital nomads from outside the EU, requires a net monthly income of at least 3,000 euros ($3,370). Coworking space Liftoff in Budapest is located in a former elevator factory, where elevators for the Hungarian Parliament Building were made. Liftoff Coworking There are around 35 co-working spots in central Budapest, according to the Coworking Hungary Association, several of which are in the bustling District VI, near the fashionable bars and restaurants of the Jewish Quarter. Alongside these hubs, the city offers around 35 serviced offices, including locations from larger providers such as Regus and DBH Flex. "Budapest has its own vibe," said Áron Levendel, a founder of co-working space Kaptar, which is within view of the city's striking St Stephen's Basilica. "Whoever wants to connect, make friends or meet people, has an easy job. Whoever wants to have fun, learn or get experiences in English, will have the challenge of choosing from hundreds of options every evening," he said. 'Community' offices Levendel and his co-founders are organizational developers who wanted a workplace that was both sociable and professional. In 2010, they came up with the idea for Kaptar (the word means "hive" in Hungarian). "Gmail was already there, but most of the work was not in the cloud or online yet; people had folders and papers. Digital nomads were not a thing," Levendel told CNBC by email. "Co-working" also wasn't a term in common use at the time, so he called the space a "közösségi iroda," or community office. Since the Covid-19 pandemic, Kaptar has grown more than 30% every year, according to Levendel, including a "wave" of digital nomads who joined after the pandemic, often arriving initially for a month but staying for up to a year. Overseas members either keep an existing job and work remotely, or they are freelancers who can travel, Levendel said. Gyurity expects the digital nomad trend to continue, noting that AI now allows individuals to create and launch services or businesses without the resources of a large organization. "More people will be able to imagine their knowledge, skills and opportunities outside the traditional corporate world," she said. At the same time, she recommends that those in the corporate world spend time in a co-working environment. "Most people are there because they are trying to solve something," she said. "Every day I meet younger people who are at a very different stage of their lives and careers, use different tools, and approach problems differently. We can learn from each other." items.title: Get Out From Behind Your Desk: 5 Tips On Making Senior Management
items.description: Greystar Director Emily Papworth laid out the stark facts at Bisnow ’s Women Leading Real Estate event this month: 44% of those at middle management level in UK property are women, but that figure drops to just 26% when it comes to senior management. Jo McNamara taking the top spot at British Land is a positive example of a woman occupying one of the highest-profile jobs in UK property. But as a whole, the industry still lags when it comes to diversity. There is no silver bullet to change that, but the event featured a plethora of advice for those looking to progress their career to the top levels. Embrace Complexity And Find Your Niche Bisnow/Daniel Sikpi Mishcon de Reya's Anju Suneja and Mirastar's Ekaterina Avdonina Mirastar CEO Ekaterina Avdonina is a rare example of a female founder and CEO in property, having set up the specialist logistics investment and development platform in 2019, after founding Delin Properties in 2011. Avdonina said logistics, traditionally one of the most male property subsectors, appealed to the logical brain of someone who actually grew up in a family of rocket scientists. Logistics is a global business where occupiers consider specific location, transport, infrastructure links, labour, real estate and the long-term plans around the investments in those buildings. “That complexity really inspired me, and it was worth specialising,” she said. You Won't Succeed Sat At A Desk The work senior leaders do is different to that of middle management and the general workforce. A lot less of it is done from behind a computer. “The work is different, and that's probably been the biggest pivot for me over the last 18 months,” said Nisha Kerai, Legal & General head of operations and asset management for build-to-rent and purpose-built student accommodation. “When I go into the office, I make time to walk around and understand what's going on in the business, what will add value to the business, and thinking about new ideas, because it's not your job to do the ‘do’ anymore.” Advice Helps You Prepare, But Advocacy Helps You Progress Bisnow/Daniel Sikpi L&G's Nisha Kerai, Kennedy Wilson's Lottie Outen, Workman's Vicky Cotton, Ogier's Katharine Marshall and BDO's Rebecca Jones Before working for Kennedy Wilson , Lottie Outen, now managing director, advised the U.S. investor in her previous role as an investment banker at J.P. Morgan . Previous Kennedy Wilson Europe CEO Mary Ricks wanted to hire Outen and pushed for the appointment internally, giving her the opportunity to step up to what Outen described as the next level. “The difference here is that it wasn't just her advice that was beneficial — it was her willingness to put her credibility behind me and make that move happen,” Outen said. “Don't just try to recognise talent, but actually try to create opportunity for it.” Don't Presume Everyone's The Same How to bring people back into a company after a career break, be that maternity or care leave or a sabbatical, is one of the thorniest issues in the corporate world — it remains one of the key barriers for women attaining senior leadership positions, panellists said. Executive coaching provided by companies can be a big help for individuals, L&G’s Kerai said — there is no reason to presume people will be able to negotiate a period they have never experienced before. But there is also the need to appreciate there is no one-size-fits-all solution for a situation that affects everyone differently. “You want to be solutions-driven, so you're jumping to what you think you would want in their shoes. You're not in their shoes,” Ogier partner Katharine Marshall said. “So the most important thing, actually, is to listen to them.” Be Loud Loud people tend to get what they want in companies, Kerai said, so don’t be afraid to speak up. “I ask for a pay rise and a promotion every six months, full year, midyear, and people laugh when I say this,” she said. “But the worst that's going to happen is somebody says no, and then the second time they say no,” she added, pointing out that there has never been any negative impact on her career. “They might even say no four times, but they'll be embarrassed the fifth time. So you'll probably get what you want at that point.” Likewise, she said, there is value in getting loud for someone else, like directing the conversation back to someone being talked over in a meeting or advocating for someone who is being overlooked for promotion because they are not putting themselves forward. items.description: While Las Vegas drowns in unsold homes and priced-out buyers sit on the sidelines waiting for lower mortgage rates , the luxury rental sector is booming, fueled by visiting celebrities, professional athletes, and out-of-town millionaires eyeing a permanent move. In October, Las Vegas’ overall housing inventory reached an all-time high of nearly 11,450 units, up roughly 10% compared to a year ago, as mortgage rates topping 7% left many buyers priced out. Yet at the very top of the local rental market, the exact opposite is happening. Local brokers say that demand for rental mansions in Las Vegas and neighboring Henderson, NV , priced between $50,000 to $100,000 per month is severely outstripping supply. "In the ultraluxury rental space, there's a huge shortage," Natalia Harris , global real estate adviser with Las Vegas Sotheby's International Realty , tells Realtor.com® . There are currently fewer than 10 super-luxury rentals on the market. "We personally, day to day, feel the frustrations of the shortage of the inventory of these rentals, because we get requests and we can't even keep up with them." Harris and her husband, fellow Sotheby's adviser Ben Harris , have been actively encouraging developers and investors to create more extravagant rental inventory to keep up with demand. Well-heeled medium-term renters, including NFL stars and elite entertainers with $1 million-per-show residencies on the iconic Vegas Strip, are not just looking for a place to sleep. They crave complete privacy, top-of-the-line accommodations, and customized features ranging from branded basketball courts to on-site tour bus hookups. Alongside celebrity renters, the Harrises often work with out-of-town executives and entrepreneurs who are considering a relocation to Las Vegas but are not sure where exactly to put down roots. "They're renting for a year maybe, or six months, while they're browsing and shopping for a home and figuring out where they want to be," says Natalia. This class of clients gravitates toward rentals in the $50,000- to $60,000-per-month bracket. While in the past the biggest feeder market for high-end rentals in Vegas was California , Natalia says over the past year, momentum has shifted to Seattle. Wealthy Washington residents are increasingly eyeing tax-friendly Nevada following the recent passage of the "millionaires tax"—a 9.9% state income tax on earnings exceeding $1 million a year. items.description: A look at how apartment REITs did in Q3 Concessions continued to dampen earnings, but bright spots in San Francisco and New York City boosted a number of companies. Published Nov. 12, 2026 Leslie Shaver Senior Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print Add us on Google Getty Images In the fall of 2023, apartment REITs sounded the alarm during their earnings calls. The glut of apartment deliveries in many markets across the country was driving massive concessions from merchant developers. In turn, public apartment companies had to drop prices, even on older assets that normally don’t compete with new supply. Analysts ended up downgrading some of those companies. “This dynamic and its impact on our B-quality communities, in particular, was unexpected and unprecedented in my 30 years in the multifamily industry,” UDR CEO Tom Toomey said on the Highlands Ranch, Colorado-based REIT’s third-quarter 2023 conference call. Three years later, in Q3 2026, supply pressures are still popping up in unexpected ways, especially for Sun Belt-centric REITs. For instance, Camden Property Trust lowered its 2026 same-store revenue guidance. September performance, in particular, surprised the company and set the stage for that revision, according to CEO Alex Jessett. “It was a greater decline in traffic than we had expected,” he said. “And when we had the decline in traffic, obviously, you have to reduce your prices if you’re trying to increase traffic.” Despite continued issues with concessions, there were many bright spots in the REIT Q3 2026 earnings reports, including strength in San Francisco and New York City. Read on for a look at results reported over the last couple of weeks. items.description: Legendary hospitality brand Waldorf Astoria has chosen a neighborhood ten minutes from downtown Denver for its first foray into residential living in Colorado . Located at 185 Steele Street, with 37 private residences ranging from studios to penthouses, Waldorf Astoria Residences Cherry Creek is slated to open in early 2028. With architecture by SAR+, interiors by BAMO, and conceptual design by Carlos Ott, prices start at $1.5 million for a studio and cap out at $13 million for the largest penthouse. While the luxury leader could have set down in a high-end ski haven like Aspen , Vail, or Telluride, the company instead went with Cherry Creek , a dense, walkable retail corridor five miles from the center of Denver. The neighborhood's median price per square foot is $293, according to Realtor.com data, compared to $334 for the overall Denver metropolitan area. Loading... ARX Creative Featuring two major commercial destinations—Cherry Creek North and Cherry Creek Shopping Center—the global brand felt this was the place to make its residential debut in the Rocky Mountain state. The brand's housing portfolio is set to nearly triple, reaching 34 properties and 3,498 units by 2030, according to the company . Residences are particularly clustered in Florida , with condo buildings in Pompano Beach, St. Petersburg, Sarasota, and Miami. Other locations include New York City; Atlanta, GA; Chicago, IL; Las Vegas, NV; Park City, UT; and Maui, HI. Cherry Creek, in a small, dense 16-block radius, may seem an unexpected choice to join in this world renowned group of cities, but the developer says it as an easy decision. Loading... Amenities include a resort-style rooftop pool with bar and lounge areas. ARX Creative "We recognized early on that Denver was ready for a world-class, branded luxury residential offering, and Cherry Creek was the natural fit," Ryan Shear, managing partner at developer Property Markets Group (PMG) , told Realtor.com. The custom Boffi kitchens include natural stone countertops and Sub-Zero and Wolf appliances. items.title: Construction site next to fatal Brooklyn collapse previously violated stop-work order: DOB
items.description: Construction site next to fatal Brooklyn collapse previously violated stop-work order: DOB The Wednesday incident killed eight people, including two construction workers, said New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. He vowed the city would hold the responsible parties accountable. Published Nov. 12, 2026 Zachary Phillips Senior Editor Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google A member of the Fire Department of New York on Nov. 12, 2026, at the clean up of a partial building collapse from the day before. The incident in Brooklyn, N.Y., killed eight people. Michael M. Santiago via Getty Images First published on Listen to the article 4 min This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback . Construction at the Brooklyn, New York, jobsite that caused the fatal building collapse Wednesday had previously violated a stop-work order from the New York City Department of Buildings. The collapse killed eight people, including two construction workers, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said during a press conference Thursday. Eighteen more were injured. On March 20, the agency filed a stop-work order and a violation on the site during project demolition when inspectors found inadequate overhead protection for some of the surrounding properties in the Flatbush neighborhood, DOB shared with Construction Dive via email. When inspectors followed up on April 23, they found demolition work had resumed, the DOB said, resulting in another violation. On May 8, the DOB lifted the order as a result of the project team correcting the violating conditions. Following the collapse, Mamdani vowed to hold any responsible parties accountable. “There are five main entities involved with this construction site who are associated with approximately 100 other sites across the city. Our Department of Buildings is commencing sweeps of those sites today,” Mamdani said. “And I will just underline: if there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable.” The DOB has issued another stop-work order as a result of Wednesday’s collapse. The order said the jobsite had “unsafe construction operations causing” the collapse. Permits reviewed by Construction Dive filed for the project list Robert Fischman of W6 Facility X as the owner and Cheng-Yi Lin Architecture as the architect of record. Fischman and Cheng-Yi Lin Architecture could not be reached for comment by the time of publication. Construction in close quarters Experts emphasized to Construction Dive that intensive building work in the crowded city is commonplace. Joe DiPompeo, president of New Jersey-based civil engineering firm Structural Workshop, said he could see that supportive excavation had been installed next to a large hole adjacent to the site. That’s a necessary practice, particularly in the Big Apple, which he said is mostly “tight buildings one on top of the other.” “There’s nothing unusual about digging a hole next to a 100-year old brownstone townhouse in the city,” DiPompeo said. He dismissed speculation that crews performing excavation work may have directly damaged the neighboring building. “People that aren’t used to dense urban construction are jumping on this. ‘They were digging next door,’” DiPompeo said. “But what they were doing here, there’s probably 500 other sites in the city that got the same thing going on.” That said, DiPompeo also underscored the value of proper shoring support in a dense construction environment. “If the supportive excavation, the soil bracing were to fail or not do what it was supposed to do, the building that fell into the hole would fall into the hole exactly the way it did,” he told Construction Dive. Timothy Hegarty, construction lawyer and partner at Zetlin & De Chiara, said New York City’s robust building codes exist for a reason. “We’ve got new construction frequently that takes place inches from century-old buildings, so the margin of error can be extraordinarily small,” Hegarty said. The good news, Hegarty said, is tragedies like Wednesday’s are uncommon on account of the due diligence builders typically apply to these jobs. Continued recovery The Fire Department of New York remains in a search and rescue mode, said Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore during Thursday’s press conference. Mamdani took time to thank the first responders, but also noted the bravery of building crews caught in the initial collapse. “Construction workers who had only barely survived themselves turned back and dug victims out of the rubble,” Mamdani said during Thursday’s press conference. “People are alive today because of their heroism yesterday.” Recommended Reading Brooklyn building collapses into adjacent construction site, leading to multiple deaths Construction Dive Add us on Google Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Filed Under: Development

items.title: The Party's Not Over at The Village Dallas
items.description: Live Poll As a Gen-Zer, I missed the Mark Cuban-, sexual revolution-era of The Village Dallas by about 25 years. Back in the 1970s and ‘80s, the now 300-acre mixed-use apartment and lifestyle community Greenville Avenue was a 21-and-up, singles-only complex that thrived on the residents’ youth and sheer will to party—hard. But despite welcoming children and monogamists to the various complexes that make up The Village 38 years ago, it doesn’t seem that it’s slowed down much on the party front. Publications The Day the Village DIED! Now that a new law forbids all-adult apartment complexes, it’s goodbye to relentless partying, mindless hedonism, and all those other things that make single life worth living. By Brad Bailey | November 1, 1988 | 12:00 am When my dad first visited me my freshman year at TCU, he found the easy, almost non-existent transition between the university’s campus and the city of Fort Worth endearing. He was amused by the row of restaurants and coffee shops lined up neatly along University Drive, punctuated by the TCU bookstore occupying the corner of an intersection also home to a gas station, bank, and Kroger. Yes, it was like our own little fake city in which we could safely test the waters of adulthood, all within a bubble encompassing just a few square blocks. I see The Village as a similar bubble. (Though, perhaps with less mocking than my dad.) Like the TCU campus and its immediate area, villagers don’t need to stray for most necessities—food, exercise, lounging. Even better, they don’t need to venture out to Lower Greenville or Knox Henderson for a good time. As my fiancé, Joel, and I pulled up to The Village for our overnight stay this Halloween, I wasn’t sure if an area so serene could get as rowdy as people claim it once was. We stayed at The Terraces, a recently opened extension of The Drey Hotel whose interior design strikes a good balance between grandeur and comfort. Children played in the baseball field while duos spilled out of the on-site pickleball court, and I wondered if we had accidentally overshot Dallas and instead landed in a leasing office catalogue. We ate like royalty at Meridian , the youngest diners among several sophisticated, Fortune 500-looking patrons. I slurped my singular chilled smoked clam politely, washing it down with a white wine I let Joel pick for us rather than a cocktail, because, well, wine just seemed to fit the vibe. That night, as we slipped into our costumes for the Nightmare on Main Street Fest, I wondered if a community so well-oiled and refined in the daylight had the capacity to unwind in the night. Free with registration was a sprawling bash at the center of the development, packed with vampires, superheroes, and Joel and me, who were moonlighting as Padmé and Anakin from Star Wars . Lightsaber and blaster pistol in hand, we were thrown right into the festivities the second we stepped outside the front doors of The Terraces. A Village Beach Club view from the DJ booth. courtesy of The Village Gone was my chill getting-ready playlist I had played through the—Terraces-provided!—Marshall Bluetooth speakers. They were replaced by the DJ's set booming through 8-foot-tall speakers set up outside the closed doors of Meridian. Just hours ago, this area was barely buzzing with a small crew setting up for the night. Now, several DJs attracted hordes of costumed dancers, live scare actors roamed foggy paths just off Main Street, and, tucked deeper in the main party was The Village Beach Club, known for its swim-up bar, daybeds and cabanas, sandy beach lounge, and an elevated stage that would soon host the night’s main entertainer. Bryce Alakai, half of one of Love Island USA ’s most beloved winning couples , was set to DJ at the Beach Club, and I desperately hoped his counterpart, Trinity Tatum, would be there, too. After a flash of a green wristband, Joel and I took our drinks from the inside portion of the Beach Club to the outside, where a small crowd had already gathered at the stage to enjoy the opening DJ. I noticed a sudden slope in my stride and suspiciously eyed the cylindrical cement seating at the nearest bar. “Are we in the pool?” Joel asked as I looked up at Clark Kent and Lois Lane atop a wall 4 feet above my head. Yes, we were in the deep-ish end of a drained pool. We took a seat on an exposed step of the empty bowl, enjoying the elevated people-, ghost-, and character-watching as oversized wings and flowing capes swirled around us. By the time Bryce actually took to the booth, I had successfully wedged us about five rows back from the stage. Aptly, we stood between a gaggle of rowdy angels and a red-horned, pitchfork-wielding couple about my age with their tongues down each other’s throats. In the best way, Bryce’s set and the atmosphere of The Village threw me briefly back to college. No, the family tenants had not wrecked The Village’s capacity for partying hard, as I saw it. In fact, all Hallow’s Eve proved its persistence. I recognized my fellow Love Island watchers as cheers tore through the crowd for Trinity (Brinity!), who emerged behind the booth as I so hoped she would. Joel and I honestly only lasted in the thick of the sweaty rave for about an hour, retiring to the less-cramped loungers on the sand for the rest of the set. Unlike college, when my night ended in a Fetii ride back to my deteriorating off-campus apartment, my nightmare on Main Street culminated in a two-minute walk back to our room at The Terraces, where I promptly shimmied into an impressively thick bathrobe and executed my nightly skin care routine in front of a ring-lighted mirror hanging from the ceiling. And as I sank into the humongous bed right around when the clocks fell back to Standard Time, Joel pulled out a delicious surprise for me. items.description: Why insurance and property taxes are becoming Houston’s biggest housing obstacles by Houston Agent November 13, 2026 Anne Hartnett Hi, I'm Anne Hartnett and I am here with real estate economist Matthew Gardner to chat about our Q3 update. How are you, Matthew? Matthew Gardner I am well, Anne, how are you? Hartnett I'm great, thanks. So we've been waiting years for housing transactions to recover. At what point do we stop calling this a cyclical showdown and recognize that something more fundamental has changed in how Americans buy and sell homes? Gardner Great question. I mean, the short answer, as far as I'm concerned, is that we should have stopped calling it a cycle, or cyclical, about a year ago, because the forces that are holding sales down now aren't really the kind that are cycle-fixes. So let me explain. When existing home sales, we know, fell from over 6 million a year in 2021 to about 4 million in 2023, and they've been stuck there for nearly three years now. September numbers came in at 3.99 million. Now, there are three structural forces that explain this: One, the mortgage rate itself has become an asset that people just won't sell. I mean, in the second quarter, 49% of outstanding mortgages carried a rate at below 4%. Now, a record 43% were originated between mid-2019 and mid-2022. That means that selling gives up that loan — and that's not a cycle. It's a balance sheet decision, and it decays very slowly. There are some who suggest that the share of mortgages at 6% or higher, which is around 22.5% in Q2, only hits 27% to 29% by mid-2027. That's a slow grind. Now secondly, the buyer pool has aged. Last year, a typical first-time buyer was 40 years old, and a typical repeat buyer was 62. And last year, first-time buyers were 21% of purchases. That's a record low, and roughly half of their pre-2008 share. And a market that runs on equity rather than income, well, it transacts less often. And finally, the ten year Treasury, it's running around 5% today, and the 3% mortgage was a product of a zero-rate world that no reasonable forecast brings back. But this year, it gave us a small test of my belief. Briefly, back in February, mortgage rates dropped to below 6%, just. I think it was at the end of February. Lowest rate since 2022. But by June, they were back up to 6.5. Now they're above 7.3. Now, at that point, when they were very low, NAR had forecast a 14% jump in sales. But what are we doing today? We're running below last year. So the dip was far too brief to prove anything by itself. But in a normal cycle, cheaper money brings buyers back fast. This time it didn't. So the bottom line for me is that 6 million sales a year is the wrong benchmark. 2021 was an anomaly — a once-in-50-year financing, or refinancing, window. In 2019, we sold about 5.3 million existing homes. And my view is that the realistic norm, at least for the rest of this decade? Somewhere between 4 and 4.5 million. And we'll get there through life events such as job changes, divorce, death, downsizing, not through a rate rally. So for brokers, that changes their business model. In a 4 million-unit market, well, the pipeline isn't buyers waiting for rates to fall. It's people who have to move regardless of rate — relocations, estate sales, divorces, retirees. Now those transactions happen at 7%. If your marketing is built around a quote, wait for rates to drop, unquote, well, you're building for a market, unfortunately, that may not show up. Hartnett Housing drives everything from construction and lending to consumer spending. Could several years of depressed transaction volume begin to weigh on broader economic growth? Gardner It already has, but interestingly, not in the way that most people assume. So let's start with what counts. The sale of an existing home is just a transfer of an asset. It doesn't add to GDP or growth. What counts is construction, remodeling and also the services around a transaction — that would be brokerage commissions, and also households buying new furniture, new appliances, that follow any move. Residential investment is only 3.7% of GDP against a historic average of about five. Now, housing’s total share of the economy? About 16%. That's actually still the lowest we've seen since 2019. Now, residential investment shrank for five straight quarters, falling at an annual rate of about 7.8% in Q1. It did tick up a bit in the second quarter. So no doubt housing has been a drag. But the contrarian part is that the economy grew right through it. Nonresidential investment rose 8.5% in the second quarter, driven by AI equipment and also software. Consumer spending rose 3.4%. You see, homeowners are sitting on substantial equity, and that wealth supports spending even when they don't move. Low transactional volumes is a slow leak, not a recession trigger. Now the real risk, as I see it, is actually different. Housing's historically been the economy's shock absorber. A recession hits the Fed cuts rates to stimulate the economy, ultimately mortgage rates drop, housing turns and construction hiring leads to a recovery. Now that channel’s impaired. Ten-year treasury near five, inflation at 3.4, and in early October, markets are still weighing whether the Fed's next move could be to hike in order to address inflation. So we may not get the usual housing-led rebound on the other side. Now where you feel the drag first is local and also sectoral. It's not in GDP. recent_coverage.title: Crescent Completes 146-Unit Melissa BTR Community

recent_coverage.title: Trademark And Morgan To Build Luxury Apartments In Oak Lawn: The DFW Deal Sheet

recent_coverage.title: Grange MPC begins second phase of development

recent_coverage.title: Pro-housing coalition presses Senate on BAAJA permitting reforms

recent_coverage.title: Larkspur Capital Begins Leasing 219-Unit Multifamily Project in Dallas

recent_coverage.title: Residential Building Worker Wage Growth Rebounds, but Real Wages Continue to Decline

recent_coverage.title: 'Certainty Will Be The Buzzword': Stability, Not Sea Change, For CRE Post-Midterm

recent_coverage.title: loanDepot's Q3 loss grows while it chases 2027 break-even

recent_coverage.title: NAR membership proves more resilient than expected, topping 1.46 million
recent_coverage.summary_zh: NAR 透露，截至 9 月会员数为 1,469,127 人，较预算高 22%，且现金与投资保持稳健，可满足即将到期的和解付款并继续投入会员产品服务。

recent_coverage.title: Berkadia Provides $219M in Agency Permanent Loan for Upper Manhattan Affordable Housing Community

recent_coverage.title: The Latest Shift in How Appraisals Are Handled Could Save Homebuyers Hundreds in Closing Costs—Eventually
